cells.tense: The private scale is steady, and the person across from you gets weighed as fairly as anyone.
cells.act: collect the fruit of the patient wait
cells.ask: Go back to something you waited out — a slow repair, a stretch you let run — and name what it actually gave you. No fixing. Just the yield, counted once.
cells.core:
There's a scale inside you that doesn't perform. It reads what's fair, what's owed, what somebody deserves, and it does the reading without making a show of it. Beside someone, that steadiness makes room: you can feel with them and still keep their measure honest. Nothing turns sentimental on your watch.

Some of what that scale weighed has finished. A stretch you waited out, a person you stayed level with, a situation you let take its course. The yield is sitting there uncollected. Gather a little of it this week — a finished thing, an honest look at what it gave you. Not a verdict. The fruit, picked.
cells.sheetLine: The scale stays honest, and you can still feel with someone.
cells.verb: weighing what is fair and what is owed, in private
cells.place: beside someone, feeling with them rather than about them

cells.tense: The scale is already checking a fairness that hasn't happened, running the numbers in advance.
cells.act: hold someone else up with what you have
cells.ask: Choose one person carrying something heavy, and give them something solid this week — a ride, a meal, an hour. Do it, finish it, and skip the review after.
cells.core:
You can feel what's fair for someone before they've said a word, and right now that reading runs past the situation. You're pre-weighing outcomes, pre-counting who will owe what, bracing for a fairness that hasn't arrived. It looks like care. From across the table, it can land as a verdict on a day that hasn't come.

Your strength is real, and it's built to move. Put it where somebody is actually standing: one person, help done and finished this week. Not balanced against anything. Not entered on the scale after. Let your strength leave your hands without the ledger following it out.
cells.sheetLine: You're pre-weighing a fairness that hasn't happened yet.
cells.verb: weighing what is fair and what is owed, in private
cells.place: beside someone, feeling with them rather than about them

cells.tense: You're standing at the scale, and the needle has gone still under your hand.
cells.act: point to the passage you can see
cells.ask: Someone is stuck on ground you've crossed. Say the route that carried you — the actual turns, simply, once — then step back and leave them to take it.
cells.core:
You used to read a room's fairness easily. Now you're at the scale but the needle isn't moving, and beside people you're here without being in it. The connection runs thin. Not that you don't care; the instrument went quiet and you kept standing at it.

Here's the way back: you know a passage somebody else is hunting for. Not advice about their life — the route itself, the one you walked. Say it simply, once, to a person who's lost on it, and then step back. You don't have to feel your way back to the scale first. Pointing the way is how the compass finds north again.
cells.sheetLine: You're still at the scale, but the needle stopped moving.
cells.verb: weighing what is fair and what is owed, in private
cells.place: beside someone, feeling with them rather than about them

cells.tense: The fairness is being read cleanly, and it keeps getting filed under a mood.
cells.act: distinguish what is yours from what you borrowed
cells.ask: List three pulls on you right now — things you feel you're supposed to do or feel. For each, ask whether it came with you or arrived separately. Keep the ones that came with you.
cells.core:
You read what's fair between people with a precision you don't take credit for. It lands as a feeling — who's owed, who's being shorted, what the room actually needs — and it gets folded under 'just a sense I have.' The reading is accurate. The byline is missing.

Some of what you're carrying was not yours to weigh. It arrived: a family's version of fairness, a room's expectation, an old accounting somebody else started. Sort three of them this week — the pulls on you right now — and mark which ones came with you. You don't have to put any of them down. You only have to see whose they are. That's the whole act.
cells.sheetLine: The fairness is read cleanly, and it keeps getting called a mood.

attempts.check: The draft claims the person is doing 'the moral accounting privately' — the record supports a felt-sense of fairness at the inner face, but not that accounting is their ongoing activity. A reader could reasonably say the weighing is not private or not happening at all, and the cell should let them. The asks survive being wrong: each is small, concrete, and useful whether or not the read lands. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line that tells them what their fairness work costs them — cut it.
